title: Water conveyance structures
summary: Penstock design turns on two things: the economic diameter, which balances steel cost against lost energy, and the thickness, which must be checked against the WATER HAMMER pressure and not merely the static head. For tunnels, the rock mass classification systems (RMR and Q) and the support types are the examinable content, with the Himalayan problems of squeezing ground and high water inflow as the practical context. Anchor blocks resist the thrust at every bend, and expansion joints between them are what prevents thermal buckling.

sections.heading: Choosing the conveyance
sections.body:
**The options between the headworks and the powerhouse:**

| Conveyance | Character |
|---|---|
| **Open canal** | Free surface; follows the contour |
| **Flume** | An elevated channel, in concrete or steel, crossing a gully or unstable ground |
| **Low-pressure pipe** | Buried or surface pipe carrying the headrace flow |
| **Free-flow tunnel** | A tunnel with a free water surface |
| **Pressure tunnel** | Flowing full under pressure |
| **PENSTOCK** | The final **high-pressure** conduit to the turbine |

**Canal or tunnel** for the headrace — the decision that shapes the project:

| | **Canal (surface)** | **Tunnel** |
|---|---|---|
| Capital cost | **Lower per metre** | **Much higher** |
| Alignment | Must follow the contour, so it is **long** | **Short and direct** |
| Head loss | Higher (longer, and a rougher surface) | Lower |
| **Vulnerability** | **Landslides, rockfall, monsoon damage, erosion of the outer bank** | **Protected from all surface hazards** |
| Geological risk | Low | **HIGH — the principal cost risk** |
| Maintenance | Regular, but accessible | Minimal, but access requires a shutdown |
| Land acquisition | Along the whole length | Portals only |
| Construction time | Shorter | Longer |

**Nepali practice has moved toward tunnels**, and the reasoning is worth stating plainly: a hillside canal on the steep, weak slopes of the Middle Hills is a **recurring liability** — damaged in every monsoon, sometimes destroyed by a landslide, and requiring an access track along its whole length for maintenance. The tunnel's higher capital cost buys **reliability for the plant's life**, and its shorter alignment recovers part of the cost in reduced head loss and reduced land acquisition.

The trade is therefore **geological risk at construction against operational risk for fifty years** — and since the operational risk recurs annually while the geological risk is incurred once and can be investigated, the tunnel usually wins for any scheme of significant capacity.

**Free-flow or pressure tunnel:**

| | Free-flow | Pressure |
|---|---|---|
| Water surface | **Free**, at atmospheric pressure | **Full**, under pressure |
| Lining | Often unlined or lightly lined | **Lined**, and checked for internal pressure |
| Grade | Must follow a **hydraulic gradient** | Can follow any convenient grade |
| Surge protection | A **forebay** at the end | A **surge tank** |
| Suits | Long headrace at low pressure | Where the alignment must dip, or the head is applied |

**A pressure tunnel must satisfy the rock cover criterion**, which is the governing check: the **weight of rock above** must exceed the **internal water pressure**, or the tunnel will hydraulically jack the rock and leak. The usual requirement is that the rock cover be at least about **0.4 to 1.0 times the static head**, depending on the rock quality and the topography — and it is critical near the **portals and under valley sides**, where the cover is least. A steel lining is provided where the criterion cannot be met.

sections.heading: Tunnels
sections.body:
**Rock mass classification** — the basis of support design, and both systems are examinable:

| System | Parameters |
|---|---|
| **RMR (Rock Mass Rating, Bieniawski)** | **Uniaxial compressive strength**, **RQD**, **joint spacing**, **joint condition**, **groundwater**, and a correction for **joint orientation** |
| **Q-system (Barton)** | **Q = (RQD/J_n) × (J_r/J_a) × (J_w/SRF)** |

**The Q-system's structure is worth understanding**, because each ratio expresses a physical idea:

| Ratio | Represents |
|---|---|
| **RQD / J_n** | The **block size** — degree of jointing |
| **J_r / J_a** | The **inter-block shear strength** — joint roughness against alteration |
| **J_w / SRF** | The **active stress** — water pressure against stress reduction |

**RQD (Rock Quality Designation)** is the underlying index:

> **RQD = (Σ lengths of core pieces ≥ 100 mm) / (total core run length) × 100%**

| RQD | Rock quality |
|---|---|
| 0 – 25% | **Very poor** |
| 25 – 50% | Poor |
| 50 – 75% | Fair |
| 75 – 90% | Good |
| 90 – 100% | **Excellent** |

**Support types**, matched to the rock class:

| Support | Function | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Rock bolts / anchors** | **Bind the rock mass together**, so it supports itself | Good to fair rock |
| **Shotcrete** (plain or **fibre-reinforced**) | Seals the surface, prevents loosening, provides a thin arch | Fair rock; combined with bolts |
| **Wire mesh** | Retains small loose fragments | With shotcrete |
| **Steel ribs / lattice girders** | Carry substantial load | **Poor rock**, squeezing ground |
| **Forepoling and spiling** | Support ahead of the face | Very poor ground |
| **Concrete lining** | Final lining; smooth hydraulic surface; carries internal pressure | Pressure tunnels; poor rock |
| **Steel lining** | Where internal pressure exceeds the rock's confining capacity | Near portals, high-pressure reaches |

**The rock bolt is the most instructive support type**, because it works by a different principle from the others: rather than **carrying** the rock, it **binds the jointed mass into a coherent beam or arch that carries itself**. That is why bolting is so economical in reasonable rock, and why it fails in ground so broken that there is nothing to bind.

**Himalayan tunnelling problems** — the practical context for Nepal:

| Problem | Character and response |
|---|---|
| **SQUEEZING ground** | Weak rock under high stress **deforms inward over time**, closing the excavation. Response: **yielding support** (deformable), a **larger excavated profile** allowing for the closure, and sequential excavation |
| **HIGH WATER INFLOW** | Sudden inrush from a fractured zone; delays and floods the works. Response: **probe drilling ahead**, **pre-grouting**, drainage |
| **Shear and fault zones** | Very weak, water-bearing; the most dangerous conditions. Response: probe ahead, heavy support, forepoling |
| **Rock burst** (in strong rock at depth) | Violent spalling under high stress | Response: destress blasting, yielding bolts |
| **Swelling ground** | Clay minerals expand on wetting | Response: seal quickly, allow for pressure |
| **High temperature** at depth | Working conditions | Ventilation and cooling |

**Squeezing ground is the characteristic Himalayan problem**, and it is worth understanding why: the rock is **young, weak and highly stressed** by active tectonics, so its strength is low relative to the in-situ stress. Rather than failing brittlely, it **creeps inward**. A rigid lining installed immediately is crushed; the correct response is a **yielding support** that permits controlled deformation while the stresses redistribute, followed by the final lining once movement has slowed. That approach — allowing deformation rather than resisting it — is counter-intuitive and is the core of modern tunnelling in weak rock (the **NATM** philosophy).

**Methods of excavation:**

| Method | Character |
|---|---|
| **Drill and blast** | Flexible, suits **variable ground and short tunnels**; the standard in Nepal |
| **Tunnel Boring Machine (TBM)** | Fast and smooth in **uniform** rock; very high mobilisation cost; **inflexible in variable or squeezing ground**, where it can become trapped |
| Roadheader | Soft rock |
| Cut and cover | Shallow depths |

**Drill and blast dominates in Nepal** for a specific reason: TBMs are efficient only over long lengths of **reasonably uniform** rock, and Himalayan geology is neither predictable nor uniform. A TBM meeting a major shear zone or squeezing ground can be **jammed for months**, whereas a drill-and-blast heading can change its support and method within a single round. Nepal's first TBM drive (on the Bheri Babai diversion) demonstrated that a TBM can succeed there, but the choice remains dependent on the geology being adequately known.

**The excavation cycle** for drill and blast: **drill → charge → blast → ventilate → muck out → support → survey**, repeated for each round of 2–4 m. Support installed **immediately after mucking**, before the next round, in poor ground.

**Tunnel shape:**

| Shape | Suits |
|---|---|
| **Circular** | **Best structurally** for internal or external pressure, most efficient hydraulically; needed for a **TBM** |
| **D-shaped (horseshoe)** | **Easiest to excavate by drill and blast**; a flat invert for haulage; the usual choice |
| Modified horseshoe | Curved invert for higher pressure |
| Rectangular | Only in very good rock or cut-and-cover |

**The circular section is structurally best but the D-shape is easier to build**, which is exactly the practical trade — and it explains why drill-and-blast tunnels are usually horseshoe and TBM tunnels always circular.

sections.heading: Penstocks
sections.body:
**The penstock** carries water under the full head to the turbine. It is a high-value, high-consequence component: its failure releases the full flow at full pressure onto a steep hillside.

**Economic diameter — the central design decision:**

| Larger diameter | Smaller diameter |
|---|---|
| **Lower velocity, lower friction loss** | Higher loss |
| **More energy generated** over the plant's life | Less energy |
| **More steel — higher capital cost** | Cheaper |

> The **economic diameter** minimises the **sum of the capital cost of the pipe and the capitalised value of the energy lost to friction**.

The usual result is a velocity in the range **3 to 5 m/s**, and a friction loss of about **3 to 5% of the gross head**. Both are outcomes of the optimisation, not rules — a scheme with a very high tariff justifies a larger pipe, and one with expensive steel a smaller one.

Empirical formulae exist for a first estimate, but the honest method is to **compute the total cost for a range of diameters and select the minimum**, which is quick and transparent.

**Thickness — and the crucial point:**

> **t = p D / (2 σ_allowable η_joint) + corrosion allowance**

where **p must be the DESIGN pressure including the WATER HAMMER rise**, not merely the static head.

**Water hammer** for a sudden closure:

> **Δp = ρ c V**,  with **c = √(K/ρ) ≈ 1440 m/s** in water (less in an elastic pipe)

and closure is "sudden" if the valve time **t < 2L/c**. For a velocity change of only 1 m/s, **Δp ≈ 1.44 MPa — about 147 m of head**. On a 200 m head scheme that is a **70% increase** over the static pressure, and it frequently **governs the thickness**.

**Design pressure** is therefore taken as the static head plus the surge, commonly **1.2 to 1.5 times** the static head for a scheme with a surge tank, and more without one. Minimum thickness is also set by **handling and corrosion** requirements, typically **6 mm** even where stress does not require it.

**Water hammer control**, in order of preference:

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Slow closure** (governor closing time) | Reduces Δp directly — the cheapest measure |
| **Surge tank** | Converts the wave problem into a mass oscillation |
| **Pressure relief valve** | Vents the excess |
| **Air vessel** | Cushions the surge |
| Flywheel on the generator | Slows the rate of speed change |
| Thicker pipe | Accepts the pressure rather than avoiding it |

**The governor's closing time is therefore a STRUCTURAL decision about the penstock**, which is the connection worth making: the mechanical and civil designs are coupled, and a closing time chosen for good speed regulation may impose a pressure the penstock cannot carry. The two must be settled together.

**Penstock layout and its supports:**

| Element | Function |
|---|---|
| **Anchor blocks** | **Resist the resultant THRUST** at every change of direction, and at intervals on a long straight run |
| **Saddle / roller supports** | **Carry the WEIGHT** between anchors, and **permit axial movement** |
| **Expansion joints** | **Absorb thermal expansion and contraction** between anchor blocks |
| Air vent / air valve | **Admits air on draining** (preventing collapse) and releases it on filling |
| Drain valve | Empties the penstock |
| Main inlet valve | Isolation at the turbine |

**Anchor block forces** — the components that must be resolved:

| Force | Source |
|---|---|
| **Momentum change at the bend** | ρQ(V₂ − V₁), resolved |
| **Internal pressure on the bend** | pA, acting along each leg |
| **Weight component along the slope** | The pipe and water weight resolved down the slope |
| **Friction at the saddles** | Resisting movement |
| **Thermal force** where movement is restrained | — |

**The pressure term usually dominates** on a high-head penstock, and it is easy to underestimate: at a 45° bend on a 300 m head with a 1.5 m pipe, pA is of the order of 5 MN — a force requiring a substantial mass of concrete.

**Expansion joints are not optional.** Steel expands about **12 × 10⁻⁶ per °C**, so a 100 m length between anchors moves about **24 mm** over a 20 °C temperature range. Restrained, that movement generates a stress of **αEΔT = 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 2 × 10⁵ × 20 = 48 N/mm²** — enough, with the pressure stress, to buckle or overstress the pipe. **Omitting the expansion joints buckles the penstock**, and it has happened.

**Penstock materials:**

| Material | Suits |
|---|---|
| **Mild steel (welded)** | **The standard** — any head, any diameter |
| **HDPE** | **Low head, small diameter** — micro-hydro; corrosion-free and light |
| Ductile iron | Moderate head |
| **GRP / GFRP** | Corrosion-free, light; moderate pressure |
| Prestressed concrete | Large diameter, moderate head |
| Wood stave | Historic |

**HDPE for micro-hydro** deserves note as the Nepali case: for a village scheme of a few tens of kilowatts and a head of 30–60 m, HDPE pipe is **light enough to be carried in by porters**, needs **no corrosion protection**, and is **jointed by fusion** with a simple heated tool — which matters far more in a remote village than the material's modest pressure rating.

**Surface or buried penstock:**

| | Surface (exposed) | Buried |
|---|---|---|
| Inspection | **Easy** | Difficult |
| Thermal movement | Needs **expansion joints** | Restrained by the soil; fewer joints needed |
| Corrosion | Painted and visible | Needs coating and cathodic protection |
| Cost | Lower | Higher (excavation) |
| Vulnerability | **Rockfall, landslide, vandalism, freezing** | **Protected** |

**Buried penstocks are increasingly preferred in Nepal** on unstable or rockfall-prone slopes, accepting the loss of inspectability for protection from the hazards that actually threaten the pipe. The **thermal advantage** is real too: buried in soil at nearly constant temperature, the pipe barely moves, so expansion joints — themselves a maintenance item and a leak risk — can be largely dispensed with.

formulas.label: Penstock economic diameter
formulas.expression: Minimise (capital cost of pipe + capitalised value of energy lost to friction)
formulas.note: Usually gives a velocity of 3–5 m/s and a friction loss of 3–5% of gross head — outcomes, not rules.

formulas.label: Penstock thickness
formulas.expression: t = pD/(2 σ_allow η_joint) + corrosion allowance
formulas.note: p must include the WATER HAMMER rise, not just the static head. Minimum ~6 mm for handling and corrosion.

formulas.label: Water hammer
formulas.note: Only 1 m/s velocity change gives ≈147 m of head — often governing the thickness.

formulas.label: Thermal stress in a restrained penstock
formulas.note: 48 N/mm² for ΔT = 20 °C. Omitting expansion joints between anchor blocks buckles the pipe.

formulas.label: Anchor block forces
formulas.expression: momentum ρQ(V₂ − V₁) + pressure pA on each leg + weight component along the slope + saddle friction
formulas.note: The pressure term pA usually dominates on a high-head penstock.

formulas.label: Barton's Q-system
formulas.note: The three ratios represent block size, inter-block shear strength, and active stress respectively.

formulas.label: Rock Quality Designation
formulas.expression: RQD = Σ(core pieces ≥ 100 mm) / total core run × 100%
formulas.note: 0–25% very poor, 90–100% excellent. The underlying index in both RMR and Q.

formulas.label: Rock cover for a pressure tunnel
formulas.expression: Rock cover must exceed about 0.4 to 1.0 times the static head, depending on rock quality
formulas.note: Critical near portals and under valley sides. A steel lining is provided where it cannot be met.
